items.question: What do you see as the biggest change in robotics over the past year?
items.object: The robotics field’s progress over the past year
items.answer: Well, definitely everyone knows now that imitation learning just works. Also, RL walking for humanoids also seems to be working for a lot of people. And VLAs are now about—I think people are trying to scale models. Also, I think the proliferation of very cheap hardware has been exciting to see, like the community is coming together, building more stuff, and sharing a lot on Twitter. I think that is exciting. It's been probably the most exciting year yet, for sure. I think maybe the biggest game changer in my mind is that the community broadly has really advanced the goalposts beyond, I think, the academic lab setting, simple tabletop pick and place from a decade ago. And really, everyone kind of transitioned last year, I would say, to more advanced embodiment, more realistic deployment settings. A lot of players started thinking about commercialization. So, very high bars for robustness and performance and generality. I think that is really exciting because the same old canned in-lab tabletop demos that would have blown everyone's minds a year ago are just very mundane now. And I think that year of reset has made it so that any release that you see today is going to be on a humanoid or on hands or in the wild or with bi-arm. And I think that's really exciting from a technical perspective because these problems are significantly harder, and it's really exciting that everyone in the field is trying to solve this now. There's a lot of push to maybe commercialization also. There are a lot more companies, a lot of funding going into the field. And also, I think that changes how different players act and how open the state of the art becomes.

items.question: How do you assess the idea of a “ChatGPT moment” for robotics?
items.object: The idea of a ChatGPT moment for robotics
items.answer: I don't think we have gotten to ChatGPT yet. And in fact, a lot of people keep saying a ChatGPT moment for robotics, but I personally think the proliferation of robots is not going to look like that. Just because for ChatGPT, everyone could experience it because consumer hardware was everywhere. Everyone had a phone or a laptop and you could just log on and type it. But for robots, you kind of need to have a robot in order to experience a robot brain, and there aren't a lot of robots. And it is a chicken-and-egg problem. People need to know that the models are capable in order to have robots and interact with them. And also the robots need to be around first in order for the models to be capable and have the data. So, I would think we are still away from the ChatGPT moment, but at least a lot of people are thinking about scaling. So, we are definitely maybe in the scaling era of robotics.

People need to know that the models are capable in order to have robots and interact with them. And also the robots need to be around first in order for the models to be capable and have the data.
So, I would think we are still away from the ChatGPT moment, but at least a lot of people are thinking about scaling. So, we are definitely maybe in the scaling era of robotics.

items.question: How do you distinguish the progress of reasoning from the progress of actions in robotics?
items.object: The differing pace of progress in robotic reasoning and actions
items.answer: I also think that for the robotics itself, when people talk about robotics, people sometimes mean different things. I think actions are probably progressing at a lower pace than reasoning and other types of inputs. The reasoning and stuff, we can borrow a lot of it from the general vision research, and also enhance it with robotics data, and the scaling of it looks very similar to how the other modalities in large VLMs look like. But for the actions, I think they're still trying to understand how to correctly scale and how to derive the scaling laws, how to represent very well. Yeah, I also think that there is a forking where maybe one part of robotics is moving much faster, probably already very close to commercialization, and another part is still getting worked upon.

items.question: How do you see the relationship between improving intermediate capabilities in a robotics base model and pursuing end-to-end learning?
items.object: The relationship between modular robotics and end-to-end learning
items.answer: To me, I feel like it is kind of bringing together multiple contradictions in the community. So, prior to all of this work, there were groups of people who think that robotics should be cut into multiple different modes and then pieced together, like earlier self-driving and stuff, where you have perception and then you take those outputs and then there's a planning module. So, a robotic system is pieced together. And then there are people who are like end-to-end learning, where everything is neural, images in and then actions out. I feel like the effort to improve the base model with all of the intermediate-level capabilities as well as the effort to improve the base model with the final or the end-to-end type approach kind of mix. I feel like it's not one or the other solution. It can be both and both can improve each other. That was quite a realization for me.

items.question: How do you understand the trend toward fewer layers in robotics model architectures such as Gemini Robotics?
items.object: The trend toward integrating robotics capabilities into one general model
items.answer: I think maybe it was in the tech report that Gemini Robotics itself is also multiple layers in the sense that there is a cloud backbone and then there is an on-robot action decoder. I think the way things are heading is we are realizing that each of these capabilities are not very separate, and as the models become more and more general, there is a tendency to bring all of the capabilities together in one model. Just like in general language research, where people initially had specialized models and then they started coming together.

items.question: How do you think about the relationship between Gemini ER, the action model, and the division of computation between the cloud and the robot in Gemini Robotics?
items.object: The distribution and composition of Gemini Robotics models across the cloud and the robot
items.answer: So I think maybe where you are understanding it incorrectly is that the ER is in the cloud and the actions model is in the robot. That is not the correct understanding. ER is more like a version of the model that is specifically trained for ER capabilities. So the action model is in itself distributed. The action model is also on the cloud and also on the robot. At inference time we cannot assume that all the models are pinged during inference. It's like a family of models. So you can fine-tune the Gemini actions from a version of the Gemini ER, but when the robot is moving it is not necessarily that you are pinging a Gemini ER model. There are different ways to compose the models, like Ted said. Also, there are demonstrations in the paper with key-point-based methods where the model is outputting key points and then a key-point-conditioned action model is acting. And there are also ways where it's more end-to-end, where it's just a pure Gemini Robotics model. So maybe the right way to interpret it is that there is a part of work where a lot of compute is happening on the cloud. There is some compute that's really fast happening on the robot and local, and the interfaces between them are modifiable and abstractable. The type of models that you can plug in different places is also modifiable. And the bandwidth of communication is also something where you have degrees of freedom to act on.

items.question: Why do you think an end-to-end model could be the right design for physical intelligence?
items.object: End-to-end models as a design for physical intelligence
items.answer: One demonstration or demo that moved the needle for me in this release was the interaction from Dorsa, where she was interacting with the robot and it was dealing with completely unseen objects. So it would pick and place them, and then she was folding a paper plane or boat, and then talking to the robot, writing or drawing an instruction, and then the robot would do it. It kind of made me really think that robotics is an AGI-hard problem, which involves actions, multimodal understanding, language understanding, symbol understanding. And so if we have multiple models who are good at different things and then kind of orchestrated, it may not be the right kind of setup to bring about an end-to-end capability. We noticed that even in the language modeling domain, when audio became native, you got a lot more things for free, like intonations and expressions that it was harder to get from just making speech and then converting that from speech to text. I would definitely think that, depending on where your belief is, if you think that robotics can be parsed into these problems or you think there should be holistic understanding and the interfaces are blurry or not very clear, then I would think that in the end, it's all intelligence. Even motion is intelligence, and it's probably going to look like a model that's capable of a lot of different things. I don't think that the nature of physical intelligence is very different than the nature of generic digital intelligence itself. It's simply a different type of expression of them.

items.question: How do you think real-world experience should guide the design of safe, responsive robots?
items.object: Learning how to design safe, responsive robots through real-world deployment and simulation
items.answer: So, in addition to very active planning and for safety, we also need to have software systems that do operational safety on the robot and mechanisms to intervene and stuff. And I also think that getting safety right is very, very important. We are not going to know all of the answers up front, I think, or the optimal design up front. So some of it we will need to learn by doing and put the robots out there. I think that would give a lot of information about what is the latency that you need and how you deal with different situations, and also by simulating them. This year and next people are trying to push the robots out from the labs where they are in very controlled settings onto harder situations, more real-world applications. And that would be a great opportunity to learn what are the more practical limitations about the glass slipping in your hand or something. I think that would definitely guide the design.

items.question: How do you explain the dexterity of the robot control shown in the Gemini Robotics demonstrations?
items.object: Gemini Robotics’ local action decoding and high-level replanning
items.answer: Our local action decoder has a control latency of 50 hertz, and the high-level, end-to-end planning latency for the system is 250 milliseconds. So you see replanning every 250 milliseconds, but then you can also see a little bit of the fine trajectories happen at 50 hertz. That's why you see the control being really nice and dextrous.
quotes: The local action decoder has a control latency of 50 hertz, and the high-level, end-to-end planning latency for the system is 250 milliseconds. So you see replanning every 250 milliseconds, but then you can also see a little bit of the fine trajectories happen at 50 hertz. That's why you see the control being really nice and dextrous.

rubrics.text: The response explains that Gemini Robotics’ local fine-trajectory control operates at a higher frequency than its high-level replanning.

items.question: What convinced you that these robotics models represent a real step-level change?
items.object: Robotic tool use and signs of a step-level change in capability
items.answer: One thing where I was very mind-blown was using the tongs. I used to think that a lot of tool use needed hands, and ALOHA had its own strategy where you had two fingers, one gripper holding the tong and then another gripper operating it. That was really fun, and it looks a lot like maybe a human is controlling it, and maybe the strategy did come from a human, but how well and how dexterously it executes blows your mind. I think also maybe a measure of technology is how mind-blown the researchers themselves are. When people from our lab, people who worked on the models, would go and play with these, and they come back, they'd be like, 'Wow, there is something there.' I think that is a real step-level change.

items.question: Where do you see room for improvement in how robotics models combine dexterity with generalization and instruction following?
items.object: Combining robotic dexterity with generalization and instruction following
items.answer: Maybe one thing where I feel a little bit that there's room for improvement is that there is dexterity, and then there is generalization or the instruction-following results, where you can play with these models and then it's a lot of pick and place. Future work to be done is bringing both of them closer together. Even in our paper there are dexterity evals, a bunch of very fine tasks, and then there are more generalization evals. I would also think that dexterity became an area of research maybe late 2023, 2024. And now people know how to do dexterity reasonably well, and yet doing dexterity with a lot of generalization is something that needs to be more clearly measured and improved.

items.question: How do you think about the risk of catastrophic failure when testing the ALOHA tabletop robot?
items.object: Failure modes of the ALOHA tabletop robot
items.answer: I think it also depends on the testing scenarios, and ALOHA is tabletop and there are few ways to fail catastrophically or damage objects. So it mostly looks a little bit like a toddler that's learning to grasp and do things. Failure looks a lot like low success rate, where it's trying to grab and then it doesn't, so it just keeps going. I think it's never a catastrophic failure. There are a lot of modes to fail that are catastrophic. For ALOHA, what are you going to do? You're going to miss the object, but if you look at how much pressure it applies and the way it moves, there are fewer ways for catastrophic failure.

items.question: How do you understand the current state of safety in vision-language-action robot models given the Asimov benchmark’s roughly 80% safety accuracy?
items.object: Safety in vision-language-action robot models and the Asimov safety benchmark
items.answer: When we were answering the last question about how we prompt the Alohas, Ted and I questioned the models in good faith and asked them to do things. And then there's Pierre who built the Asimov benchmark, and because they questioned the models in bad faith and tried to get all these failures, they tried to get more of a sense of how badly can it fail. Right now it is kind of research. I would think that the safety of the VLA models is not quite there or evolved to the point where language-model safety has evolved. Right now the approach is more operational safety and also semantic and high-level safety. What you read in there with the 80% of the times don't pour the boiling water and maybe one out of six times do pour the boiling water, that's more like the semantic safety side of it, but that is not the only safety layer and we also need operational safety. Right now, with the way that the models are run, there are people watching it, there are e-stops, literal e-stops which would freeze the robot. So that is how we run the robots currently. Now, as we start deploying it, we need even the high-level safety to improve. And maybe we will have more safety layers that don't shroud the capability itself, that allow the capabilities to shine while also being safe. I would think it's a bit of a dance, and the measurement that you saw is more like where we are currently. Future research and deploying them into more real-world-like situations would evolve both of these parts and hopefully bring about a more balanced way to react. Like you said, safety is a long-tail problem there for a lot of machine-learning methods. So I do not see a day where we do away with more classical safety bounds on the system. Even when things are on the cloud, maybe the internet goes down or there are other things happening, or everything that can fail might likely fail in a stressful situation. So you do need guaranteed non-failing systems on the robot to help there.

items.question: How do you think about the case for deploying robots in homes before commercial settings?
items.object: Deployment of robots in homes versus commercial settings
items.answer: Thinking around that kind of differs between different groups and different companies and stuff. There are people who build robots who think that maybe we should go to the home first because it's really hard, and it's going to give us a lot of great data, and so that's where we should go first. I think there are also people who believe that homes need you to reach a very high safety bar and a very low price point. So they might likely be one of the last use cases to get solved, but you can still get a lot of generalization in other commercial settings. I think the question of the path of deployment is up to the groups deploying it and the level of risk and how they think about what's feasible. From a purely technical perspective of will the technology be ready to even deploy to these increasingly unstructured environments, I think that's maybe where I am better suited to discuss.

items.question: How do you assess real-world deployment flywheels versus in-house data collection as paths to improving robot autonomy?
items.object: Real-world deployment data flywheels versus in-house robot data collection
items.answer: One interesting question I don't have a good answer for, but I guess maybe there are two schools of thought: you need these deployments to get your data flywheels, your Tesla flywheel of generating value, people are paying for it, you're getting data, your crude models turn your flywheel, and you deploy more and more. Or do you already need to come out with a very good product from the get-go if autonomy is a core part of what you're offering? You get that through frontier modeling or through in-lab data collection. It's unclear whether you need that in-the-wild data flywheel that's going into more and more mining of the long tail, or whether you'll make faster progress by trying to get that diversity and data volume in-house. items.question: How do you think about the data needed to scale robotics capabilities?
items.object: Data for scaling robotics capabilities
items.answer: I think data is definitely a blocker to robotics progress, and the fact that you kind of need to have hardware in the loop to get the data makes things grow at a slower pace. So I definitely think with the ER style of work, exploiting internet-style data sets and maybe also distilling that into robotics capabilities is going to be really useful, and effectively using all of that human-uploaded data and simulations is going to go a long way. I want to say one thing that Ted said, which is the billion tokens. It matters where the billion tokens come from. A billion tokens of just generic pick and place on a conveyor belt is not going to solve AGI. So we do need these things to be billion- or trillion-like AGI-hard robotics tokens. What is the type of data that's coming in is going to be really important. It should not be a lot of repetitive data. It should be very diverse and high quality. And maybe a second thing is even in language-modeling research, people are now realizing that what we need is not a lot of data like we needed, but quality of the data is going to be really critical. Then you take these large noisy data sets, there's a lot of processing and deduplication, and then you look at what is the effective number of tokens that you have. I think maybe one advantage that we have in robotics going forward is that we can borrow a lot of the lessons learned from the language-modeling domain. We can think about what are the effective number of tokens and then go ahead and collect those. So we can get a lot of tokens for free from the internet or even cheaper tokens, which is simulation as a way to convert compute into data. But also for real-world collection, we can look at how to get the best data. A lot of the scaling study can also help us understand what is the best data that we should collect, what is the best data that can give coverage over capabilities, and then go ahead and collect that.

items.question: Why do you feel optimistic about combining simulation, human-generated data, and video models for robotics now?
items.object: The convergence of simulation, human-generated data, and video models for robotics
items.answer: We think of simulation as a different thing, human-generated data as a different thing, video models as a different thing. But if you look at the pace of progress in video models, it's kind of trained on large videos, a lot of internet-scale videos, but it can also generate simulations, much more steerable environments that you want. So in a way, all of these three different data sources are coming together in the video models, but is it realistic physics, and maybe we need more grounding in actual physics simulation. The worlds are coming together. And also from the other side, we are also adding the actions to look more like the real-world data. I feel like maybe this point in time is the point in time to be most optimistic about using all of these diverse sources of data.

items.question: How do you see robotics capabilities becoming available through general Gemini models?
items.object: Integration of robotics capabilities into general Gemini models
items.answer: Yeah, definitely, I think the trajectory is tending that way. A lot of work needs to be done. Especially the ER stuff, it's already getting upstreamed; you can access a lot of ER capabilities in the Gemini 2.0 Flash itself. Like supposedly you don't have access to the ER model. So, like I said, it's two-pronged, right? A lot of the ER stuff is already getting upstreamed, and because it's much closer to how the language-modeling data looks like, I think actions are going to take some more time.

items.question: How do you decide whether robotics should be built on frontier foundation models or on separate models?
items.object: Frontier foundation models as an approach to robotics
items.answer: This was one thing that I also thought very deeply about maybe 1 and 1/2 years, 1 year ago when there were a spring of robotics companies. To me the belief boiled down to: do you think robotics is an AGI problem or not? If you think it's an AGI problem, then you would want to work with the best frontier model and add the action or the movement and physical reasoning as a capability on top rather than build a separate model. One year down the line, you can see that the people who went out to build these models are now adding back in 3D bounding boxes or 2D bounding boxes to get more spatial reasoning in addition to action. A lot of people started out with collecting action data sets and now they are adding in embodied reasoning. Eventually you will see them adding in audio, interaction, Astra-like capabilities with multimodal reasoning. At that point, you are kind of re-engineering the large Gemini-like foundation model on its own. And it's very capital intensive to do so, and the market kind of consolidates into a few players. That being said, whether you think robotics is an AGI problem has helped me really reason about what type of approach can make the most progress. I thought that working with state-of-the-art frontier models was really important to make progress at the edge. And at least for the next year or two, this is going to continue to be the case. I strongly believe that, especially given the progress that we made in the last 1 year.

items.question: How do you see the opportunities for companies beyond big tech as frontier models become central to robotics?
items.object: Opportunities for companies beyond big tech in the foundation-model ecosystem
items.answer: I don't quite think this is a big-tech win or that there isn't space for players. If you look at language-modeling companies, the spring has been probably the biggest risk or change of the world order in tech in the last decade, maybe in the last 20 years. This is the biggest thing that's happening in language models. And the fact that there's so much innovation gives a space for a lot of players to win also. Like Cursor, for example, the coding experience that they give is really good and it's better than VS Studio and other things. Same with image-generation models and stuff. So I do think there's space to build amazing useful things regardless of where the model comes from. And also I'm hoping that more and more people build foundation models. A lot more players are entering and a lot of innovation and competition is just getting started. I'm very excited about it. I think it only gives more space for people to win.

items.question: How do you assess the potential for adapting robotics models to your own robot and tasks with only a few demonstrations?
items.object: Adapting robotics models with limited demonstration data
items.answer: We are seeing that with hardware that's repeatable, you can get very good performance with a very few number of demonstrations, but it also is a function of how narrowly you define the task. If you want your task to work in more general situations, now you need a little bit more data than before than if you just had narrow situations. And secondly, if you have a harder task, that also increases the amount of data that you need. But I definitely think it's possible that the models are more widely available, and then with your own specialized data, you can fine-tune it to your own robot in your house, your specific embodiment, your specific task, or your specific general scenario.

items.question: How do you understand the role of robot hardware in setting the frontier for AI capabilities?
items.object: The relationship between robot hardware and AI capabilities
items.answer: I think maybe this is the question where Ted and I have slightly different opinions. I think it comes from the fact that we were initially working on the EDR robots and then we had the Alohas, and just moving from the Meta to the Alohas made dexterity a field of research. And this was made capable because the hardware offered a frontier to really push the capabilities. So, I think of hardware as the boundary—hardware provides a playground for the AI to really push. So you can have amazing AI, but if your hardware is limiting, then it's not going to be actually able to do much.

items.question: Why do you see the move from ALOHA robots to humanoids as a step change for robotics research?
items.object: The transition from ALOHA robots to humanoids
items.answer: And now I think of ALOHA to humanoid as another step change because it gives you a lot more playground or frontier to really push research, namely multi-finger dexterity. ALOHA has the grippers, so now we have these robots with hands and you can do a lot of different things with hands. And hands, I think there's both a teleoperation problem, like how to control a higher degree-of-freedom hand, and how to control it autonomously, how to control it for teleoperated human demonstration data. So definitely that offers a new problem to solve, which is how to solve multi-finger dexterity. There's also full-body control and interfacing with oral standing controllers is a new field of study that ALOHA or other embodiments are not offering. So let's say if you have an oral-trained balancing controller, how do you get that to squat and pick up things from lower shelves or manipulate at different heights and stuff? You can do that with wheeled platforms, but the problem offered by wheeled platforms and the problem offered by legs are different. With wheels, if you lean over, it's harder to lean over. And with legs, when you lean over, you balance differently because you put one leg behind to balance your weight. I think also with humanoids, it's a much more complex platform.

items.question: How do you assess the risk of working on humanoid robots when robotics research needs data at scale?
items.object: Scaling humanoid robotics research
items.answer: Like all the grad students, it's like they're always broken down. It's much more complex, there are many parts, and getting scale is really important. Maybe there is a risk to working on humanoids: at some point you do need the type of scale that cheap platforms like ALOHAs offer you, where a lot of these VLA and other problems are now problems of scale, and you need to collect data at scale to expose yourself to problems that you would encounter at scale. So getting scale on humanoids is going to be an important problem, but I think it is an engineering problem, and we are likely to make a lot of progress on it.

items.question: How do you think researchers should approach the added complexity of scaling humanoid robot learning beyond platforms like ALOHA?
items.object: Scaling humanoid robot learning
items.answer: I think the problem is hard. My approach is we should just study it. I think this is something that we are very consciously thinking about as we scale humanoids. It is a different platform and it has much more complexity. Even at ALOHA, where we have a lot more experience, it's easier to think about how much data to collect to get how much capability. Also, you have a fixed camera and stuff. With the humanoid it's different. Sure, narrow-task imitation learning works, but I think the scaling factors are going to be different, and this is something that we need to consciously study. As we move the head, there are now different things. I also think that once you start moving the head, now your problem is no longer Markovian. You don't observe all the past states. Now you need to have some sense of memory about where you saw something, so that you don't have to search when you need to go look at the thing to grab it or something. I feel like maybe there are newer aspects that you really need in order to solve robots, like memory, for example, or a little bit more long-horizon thinking about how the world looks so that you're not always searching. I think the scaling behaviors are going to look different, but it's really important to study, and this is something that we know and are really trying to keep a pulse on as we scale the humanoids to understand these behaviors.

items.question: What improvements to robot embodiment hardware would you most like to see?
items.object: Robot hands and whole-body humanoid teleoperation hardware
items.answer: I need good hands. I think this is a problem that the community is solving. Maybe one thing I saw was in the year from last year to this year, there have been so many humanoids coming up. I also feel like there is now more investment and more people thinking about these problems, more development in the space. A lot of people are talking about it. I think Yu Ke Chu from Nvidia was also complaining that we don't have good hands on the market. That's one. Teleoperation, like on ALOHA, the teleoperation system is really simple and really good and leads to very high-quality data. But you have a person sitting here and then it's controlling an arm, and then you have another set of arms that's exactly identical, and it just copies the thing. But now you have a humanoid, you cannot do the same thing because a human is moving. So there is occlusion from different parts. If a human is standing right behind a humanoid, you can't see what the humanoid is seeing. So now you need a VR-type thing. So now you have a bunch of delays, and how to teleoperate motion-capture suits or how to do whole-body teleoperation are very open problems where I think hardware can help. Just building better humanoids, even safety is a thing.

items.question: What struck you about how people outside the AI community reacted to your Gemini Robotics release?
items.object: Public reactions to the Gemini Robotics release
items.answer: One funny reaction I got from some of my friends who are outside the AI community, when they saw our release: we put so much work into making a very great VLM and VLA for our Gemini Robotics report, but some of the reactions were, 'Oh, wow. You guys have a great humanoid and a great humanoid model, too.' I thought that was funny, that for a lot of lay people, that's the first thing they notice: 'Oh, I see a robot that looks like me and the Gemini team is working on making it smarter. That's so cool.' So I think it's super inspirational, and definitely the next year is going to be really fun for our team.

items.question: What inspires you about 1X's approach to robot hardware?
items.object: 1X's robot hardware and approach to safety
items.answer: I'm very inspired by the work that 1X is doing. I think Eric has this blog about how to think about motors for safety, how to define them so that the contact itself is low impact. From a hardware perspective also, there's a long way to go to make these robots really good enough so that you can deploy them in places, but I just want to say kudos to them. They're able to bring their robots to GTC and stuff, put a jacket on Jensen. That's really cool stuff.
